z-m-14-01.title: Going at 60 km per hour and coming back at 40 km per hour: what is the average for the round trip?
z-m-14-01.topic: Average speed of a round trip: when the distances are the same and when the times are the same
z-m-14-01.goal: Test with number examples the idea of estimating the average speed of a round trip as "the middle of the two speeds," and say how the result differs when you keep the distance the same and when you keep the time the same.
z-m-14-01.material: Mina's family went to and from Grandma's house by car on the same road. On the way there they drove at 60 km per hour (the speed of going 60 km in one hour) from start to finish, and on the way back they drove at 40 km per hour from start to finish, with no rests in between. The distance of the way there and the way back is the same. Here, the "average speed of the round trip" is the speed per hour you would have if you drove the whole road there and back at the same speed all the time. You do not yet know how many km the distance is.
z-m-14-01.thinking.0: Testing your first estimate with concrete numbers
z-m-14-01.thinking.1: Revising your judgment and confidence after seeing new information
z-m-14-01.thinking.2: Changing the distance to see whether the result changes
z-m-14-01.thinking.3: Finding the condition that the result depends on what was kept the same
z-m-14-01.prereq.0: The meaning of speed: the distance traveled in one hour (speed per hour)
z-m-14-01.prereq.1: Changing time units (1 hour 30 minutes is 1.5 hours)
z-m-14-01.prereq.2: Calculations with whole numbers and decimals (grade 5-6 level)
z-m-14-01.s.s1.prompt: Each time a piece of information is added, choose your thought about the average speed of the round trip. You do not have to change your first thought. Judge for yourself whether the evidence is enough.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, choose a distance and first find how many hours the way there and the way back each take.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.hint.1: Read the new information and compare one by one where it is the same as and different from the thought you first chose.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.info: The way there is 60 km per hour and the way back is 40 km per hour. You do not yet know the one-way distance or the time it took.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Looking only at this information, what do you think the average speed of the round trip is?
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Neither side has been confirmed yet. Choosing a distance and calculating directly will help your judgment.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is exactly 50 km per hour. This is because it is the middle of 60 and 40.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is an idea that takes the middle value of the two speeds as the average. You can test later when this idea holds.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It seems it will be less than 50 km per hour. This is because the time spent driving at the slower speed seems to be longer.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You thought not only about the speeds but also about the length of time spent at each speed.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It seems it will be more than 50 km per hour. This is because they drove faster on the way there.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You are looking only at the side that went fast. It would be good to check whether the time it took to go the same distance is the same in the two cases.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We do not know the one-way distance, so we cannot know the average speed either.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is an idea worth testing directly to see whether the distance is really needed.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Let's say the one-way distance is 120 km. The way there takes 2 hours and the way back takes 3 hours. That means they traveled the 240 km round trip in 5 hours in all.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Seeing this calculation result, what do you think about the average speed of the round trip?
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.after: When the one-way distance is 120 km, it is not 50 km per hour. Then what happens if the one-way distance is different?
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: We can consider it 50 km per hour. It is the middle of 60 and 40, so it stays the same.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You are not comparing whether the calculated result and the first estimate disagree. Compare with the value of going 240 km in 5 hours.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is 48 km per hour. They went 240 km in 5 hours, so it is as if they went 48 km each hour.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You checked the average using the total distance and the total time.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: When the one-way distance is 120 km, it is 48 km per hour. We do not yet know whether the value changes if the distance changes.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a careful judgment that, even after getting the result for one case, wants to check separately whether it is the same at other distances.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is 52 km per hour. They were faster on the way there, so it is greater than 50.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Looking at the times you calculated (2 hours and 3 hours), the slower side was driven longer. Think about how that fact shows up in the average.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.info: You also calculated with one-way distances of 60 km and 300 km. 60 km: 1 hour on the way there and 1 hour 30 minutes on the way back, so they went the 120 km round trip in 2 hours 30 minutes. 300 km: 5 hours on the way there and 7 hours 30 minutes on the way back, so they went the 600 km round trip in 12 hours 30 minutes.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Looking at all the cases where the one-way distance is 60 km, 120 km, and 300 km, how do you judge?
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.after: In all three distances tested, it is 48 km per hour. However, this does not settle the distances that were not tested.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It was 48 km per hour in all three cases. At these three distances, it was the same even when the distance changed.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You summed up the result while stating exactly the range that was tested.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The longer the distance, the greater the average speed of the round trip gets.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Put the average speed values of the three cases side by side and compare them.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: We tried it three times, so it has already been proved that it is 48 km per hour at any distance.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You settled every case with only a few tested examples. A few examples being right is different from a proof.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The average is different for each distance, so we cannot say it with a single value.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: It seems you said this without actually comparing the results of the three cases. Check the numbers again.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.info: This time, let's keep the time the same instead of the distance. On the way there they drove for 2 hours at 60 km per hour, and on the way back they drove for 2 hours at 40 km per hour. The distances in the two directions may no longer be the same.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.ask: What is the average speed of the round trip in this case?
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.after: When the distance was kept the same it was 48 km per hour, and when the time was kept the same it was 50 km per hour. The average depends on what was kept the same.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.o.a: It is less than 50 km per hour. It came out less than 50 km per hour before, so it does this time too.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.r.a: What was kept the same before (distance) and what is kept the same this time (time) are different, but you carried over the result as it was.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.o.b: We cannot tell. This is because we do not know the distance.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.r.b: This time the time is fixed, so you can find the distance traveled in each direction.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.o.c: It is 50 km per hour. This is because they went 120 km and 80 km, 200 km in all, in 4 hours.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You calculated again under this new condition (the time is the same) to check.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.o.d: It is 48 km per hour. It was 48 km per hour before, so it is the same this time.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.st.3.r.d: You applied the earlier result as it was to a situation where the condition changed. Calculate again under the changed condition.
z-m-14-01.s.s1.reflect: At first 50 km per hour seemed the most likely, but when the distance was kept the same, it was 48 km per hour. It was 50 km per hour only when the time was kept the same. Look back at which piece of information changed your judgment, or whether it did not need to change.
z-m-14-01.s.s2.prompt: Hyewon said, "The average speed of a round trip is the middle value of the two speeds." Explain, using the numbers you saw above, in which case this statement is right and in which case it is not.
z-m-14-01.s.s2.hint.0: It is fine to write just one of the two cases first.
z-m-14-01.s.s2.hint.1: Try starting the sentence with "If ... is the same."
z-m-14-01.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., For the middle of the two speeds to be right, ...
z-m-14-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can you follow, with the numbers I wrote, how the average speed becomes 48 km per hour or 50 km per hour?
z-m-14-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you separate "when the distance is the same" from "when the time is the same"?
z-m-14-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying that the middle value of the two speeds is always the average?
z-m-14-01.s.s2.model.0: For 50, the middle of the two speeds, to be right, the times driven on the way there and the way back must be the same. If the distances are the same, the way back takes longer, so more time is spent driving at the slower 40, and the average is 48, less than 50.
z-m-14-01.s.s2.model.1: If the one-way distance is 120 km, the way there takes 2 hours and the way back takes 3 hours, so they went 240 km in 5 hours, which is 48 km per hour. But if they drove 2 hours each, they went 120+80=200 km in 4 hours, so it is 50. So it depends on whether the distances are the same or the times are the same.
z-m-14-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: The number examples were written in two separate conditions.

z-m-14-02.title: Enlarging a photo to fit a frame exactly
z-m-14-02.topic: Lengthening with the same ratio and range conditions
z-m-14-02.goal: When enlarging the width and length of a photo by the same ratio, make several possible sizes within the condition of the frame size, and find the biggest one that can fit.
z-m-14-02.material: Doyun wants to print a photo that is 12 cm wide and 9 cm long bigger and put it in a frame. To keep the photo from being distorted, he has to enlarge the width and length by the same ratio. The inside size of the frame where the photo goes is 30 cm wide and 21 cm long. The whole photo must fit inside the inside size (width at most 30 cm, length at most 21 cm), and the photo must be bigger than it is now. Write lengths in cm, and one decimal place is allowed.
z-m-14-02.thinking.1: Making a solution that satisfies several conditions (ratio and range) at the same time
z-m-14-02.thinking.2: Noticing that fitting one side can make the other side overflow
z-m-14-02.prereq.0: Ratios and making equal ratios (grade 6 level)
z-m-14-02.s.s1.prompt: Doyun said, "Let's enlarge it so that the width is exactly 30 cm, the same as the inside width." Will the photo fit in the frame if we do that?
z-m-14-02.s.s1.hint.0: First find how many times bigger 12 cm has to be to become 30 cm.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.hint.1: If the length changes by that many times too, find how many cm the length becomes and compare it with the inside length of 21 cm.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.o.a: It fits. The width is the same as the inside width of 30 cm, so the whole photo fits.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.r.a: You thought it was enough to fit only the width. You did not check what happens to the length.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.o.b: We cannot tell. We cannot know until we measure the length after enlarging.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.r.b: You missed that you can find the length beforehand by using the ratio before enlarging.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.o.c: It fits. Enlarge the width to 30 cm and just shrink the length separately to 21 cm.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.r.c: You missed that if you fit the width and length separately, the shape of the photo changes.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.o.d: It does not fit. If you enlarge by the same ratio, the length goes over the inside length of 21 cm.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.r.d: You used the ratio to check how the length grows along with it when the width is enlarged to 30 cm.
z-m-14-02.s.s1.explain: When the width goes from 12 cm to 30 cm, it is 2.5 times. The length also becomes 2.5 times, 9×2.5=22.5 cm, which goes over the inside length of 21 cm, so it does not fit.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.prompt: Make three different enlarged sizes where the photo is not distorted and also fits in the frame. (width w, length h, unit cm)
z-m-14-02.s.s2.hint.0: Divide 12 cm and 9 cm into squares of the same length, and find how many squares wide and how many squares long.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a width, find the length to match the ratio, and check both conditions (at most 30, at most 21).
z-m-14-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is bigger than the original photo (12×9).
z-m-14-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The enlarged photo must be bigger than 12 cm wide and 9 cm long.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The ratio of width to length is the same as the original photo (12:9).
z-m-14-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The ratio of width to length is not the same as 12:9. The photo is distorted.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.fail.c3: It must be width at most 30 cm and length at most 21 cm to fit inside the frame.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.explain: 12:9 is the same ratio as 4:3. When the width is 4 squares, the length should be 3 squares, so you can make (16, 12), (20, 15), (24, 18), (28, 21). The biggest photo that satisfies the same ratio and fits inside the inside size is 28 cm wide and 21 cm long.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.prompt: How many cm wide is the biggest photo that can go in this frame? Explain, along with why you do not make the width 30 cm.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write what the length becomes when the width fills the frame completely.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write what the width becomes when the length fills the frame completely.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Do the width and length you wrote satisfy the ratio 4:3?
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain by comparing filling the width completely with filling the length completely?
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you finally check whether a bigger photo is possible?
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.model.0: The biggest photo is 28 cm wide and 21 cm long. If you fit the length to 21 cm, the width is 28 cm, but if you make the width 30 cm, the length becomes 22.5 cm, which goes over the inside length of 21 cm.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.model.1: The length reaches its limit first. If the length is 21 cm, it is 3 squares of 7 cm each, so the width is 4 squares, which is 28 cm. With a width of 30 cm, the length becomes greater than 21, so it does not fit in the frame.
z-m-14-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: You reached the same conclusion by dividing into squares.

z-m-14-04.title: At the amusement park, how many rides make the pass worth it?
z-m-14-04.topic: Comparing the correspondence of two ways of paying
z-m-14-04.goal: Compare two ways of paying that change with the number of rides, using a table and an expression, find that which is cheaper depends on the number of rides and where the boundary is, and sum it up as a recommendation.
z-m-14-04.material: Minseo's family chooses one of two methods at an amusement park. In Method A, you buy an unlimited pass for 20000원, and you pay nothing more no matter how many rides you take. In Method B, you buy an entrance ticket for 8000원 and pay 1500원 each time you take a ride. Minseo plans to take n rides in one day, and can take at most 20 rides a day. There is no other money needed besides the ticket price, and rides are counted one at a time.
z-m-14-04.thinking.0: Comparing the totals of two payment methods by the number of rides
z-m-14-04.thinking.1: Finding the conclusion (boundary) that changes with the conditions
z-m-14-04.thinking.2: Judging how to handle the case where they are equal
z-m-14-04.prereq.0: Calculating the total amount from the price of an item and the number of items (grade 3-4 level)
z-m-14-04.prereq.1: Putting two quantities side by side in a table to compare
z-m-14-04.s.s1.prompt: Minseo plans to take 6 rides that day. In this case, which is cheaper and by how much?
z-m-14-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write the total of Method B split into the entrance ticket price and the riding cost.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write the totals of the two methods side by side and compare them.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.o.a: Method B is 3000원 cheaper. Adding the price of 6 rides to the entrance ticket makes 17000원.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.r.a: You found the totals of the two methods with your own number of rides and compared them.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.o.b: Method A is cheaper. It is a pass for unlimited rides, so it is a better deal no matter how many rides you take.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.r.b: You did not calculate the total with the number of rides, and were drawn in by the word "unlimited."
z-m-14-04.s.s1.o.c: Method B is 11000원 cheaper. You pay only 9000원 for 6 rides.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.r.c: You left out the entrance ticket price of 8000원 and counted only the riding cost.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.o.d: The two methods are the same. Whichever you choose, it costs about 20000원.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.r.d: You did not calculate that Method B's cost grows each time the number of rides grows.
z-m-14-04.s.s1.explain: Method B is 8000+6×1500=17000원. It is 3000원 cheaper than Method A's 20000원.
z-m-14-04.s.s2.prompt: Find three different numbers of rides n for which Method A (unlimited pass) is cheaper than Method B. (n is a natural number from 1 to 20)
z-m-14-04.s.s2.hint.0: Increase the number of rides one at a time, like 6, 7, 8, 9, and write how the total of Method B changes.
z-m-14-04.s.s2.hint.1: Find the number of rides at which Method B's total is 20000원, and then compare the numbers of rides just before and after it.
z-m-14-04.s.s2.fail.c1: You can take at least 1 and at most 20 rides a day.
z-m-14-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of rides is a natural number.
z-m-14-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make the number of rides a natural number.
z-m-14-04.s.s2.ok.c3: Method A is cheaper than B.
z-m-14-04.s.s2.fail.c3: At this number of rides, Method A is not cheaper than Method B. Calculate B's total and compare it with A's 20000원.
z-m-14-04.s.s2.explain: With 8 rides, Method B is 8000+12000=20000원, which is the same as Method A. From 9 rides, B goes over 21500원 and A is cheaper. So any number of rides from 9 to 20 is a correct answer.
z-m-14-04.s.s3.prompt: Minseo's friend asked, "So which one should I buy?" Recommend how to choose depending on the number of rides, including the case where the prices of the two methods are exactly the same.
z-m-14-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write the totals of the two methods for 8 rides and for 9 rides.
z-m-14-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write sentences separately for when the number of rides is small and when it is large.
z-m-14-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you actually calculate the totals of the two methods at the boundary number of rides you mentioned?
z-m-14-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that at the number of rides where they are equal, you can choose either one?
z-m-14-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying things like "this method is always better" without mentioning the number of rides?
z-m-14-04.s.s3.model.0: If you take 8 rides, both methods are the same at 20000원. If you will take 7 rides or fewer, buying an entrance ticket and paying separately is cheaper, and if you will take 9 rides or more, the unlimited pass is cheaper.
z-m-14-04.s.s3.model.1: Up to 8 rides, paying separately is cheaper or equal, and from 9 rides the unlimited pass is cheaper. So if you think you will ride a lot, I recommend buying the unlimited pass, and if you think you will ride a little, I recommend buying only the entrance ticket.
z-m-14-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: You stated the boundary number of rides with "up to" and "from."

z-m-14-05.title: Joining 10 matchstick squares together
z-m-14-05.topic: Finding a rule and writing it as an expression (matchstick squares)
z-m-14-05.goal: Find the rule between the number of joined squares and the number of matchsticks, judge whether expressions written in different forms show the same rule, and find and fix the error in how the rule was counted.
z-m-14-05.material: Make shapes by joining squares in a row with matchsticks. You need 4 matchsticks to make 1 square, 7 to join 2 squares, and 10 to join 3 squares. Where squares touch when joined, they share one matchstick. You do not break matchsticks or lay them on top of each other.
z-m-14-05.thinking.2: Checking whether different expressions show the same rule
z-m-14-05.prereq.0: Finding the number in the next shape of a pattern with a rule (grade 5)
z-m-14-05.prereq.1: Using □ to show a relationship between numbers (grade 5-6)
z-m-14-05.s.s1.prompt: Seoyun found the number of matchsticks needed to join 10 squares as shown below. Pick the first line that is wrong.
z-m-14-05.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the case of 2 squares with the same expression and check whether it matches the actual 7.
z-m-14-05.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many times you do "add one more" to go from 1 square to 10 squares.
z-m-14-05.s.s1.line.0: You need 4 matchsticks for 1 square, 7 for 2 squares, and 10 for 3 squares.
z-m-14-05.s.s1.line.1: Each time the number of squares goes up by one, the matchsticks go up by 3.
z-m-14-05.s.s1.line.2: Then for 10 squares, it goes up by 3, 10 times from the first 4, so 4+3×10=34.
z-m-14-05.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The first 4 is already the value for 1 square, so to get to 10 squares, the number of increases is 9, not 10. 4+3×9=31 is right, and the 34 in the last line is wrong too as a result.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the expressions that correctly show the number of matchsticks needed when there are □ squares. (How to read: × is multiply, − is subtract)
z-m-14-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put 1, 2, and 3 in for □ in each expression and check whether it equals the actual numbers 4, 7, and 10.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.hint.1: Even if expressions look different, see whether some give the same number by putting the same number in for □ and comparing.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.r.a: This is an expression that counted the touching sides one extra time. When □ is 2, it gives 8, which is different from the actual 7.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.r.b: This expresses the rule of increasing by 3 each time and the first 1 separately.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.r.c: You took the overlapping sides to be □. Count how many places touch when □ squares are joined.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.r.d: You counted all the sides of each square and then subtracted the number of places that touch.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.r.e: This is an expression that fits only one or two values. Check it for 2 squares and 3 squares too.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.r.f: You expressed it by making the first square 1 first and adding 3 for each of the rest.
z-m-14-05.s.s2.explain: 1 square takes 4 matchsticks, and each time you join one, it goes up by 3. So 4+3×(□−1), 4×□−(□−1), and 3×□+1 are all the same rule. You can check by putting in 1, 2, and 3 squares to see if you get 4, 7, and 10.
z-m-14-05.s.s3.prompt: How many matchsticks are needed to join 10 squares? Explain two different ways to check that your answer is right.
z-m-14-05.s.s3.hint.0: First check with small numbers (2 and 3 squares).
z-m-14-05.s.s3.hint.1: Write how many it goes up by each time one is added, and how many places touch.
z-m-14-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are the two methods really different ways?
z-m-14-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that your expression is right with small numbers (2 and 3 squares) too?
z-m-14-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you tell apart whether the answer 31 is a value you actually counted or a value that came from an expression?
z-m-14-05.s.s3.model.0: It is 31. Each time a square is added, it goes up by 3, so adding 3 nine times to the first 4 gives 4+27=31. Also, from 4×10=40, subtracting the 9 sides that touch and are shared also gives 31.
z-m-14-05.s.s3.model.1: 31. 3×10+1=31. Counting by first placing 1 vertical side and then adding 3 for each square in a bracket shape also gives 31. It is also confirmed by subtracting the overlapping sides: 4×10−9=31.
z-m-14-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: The counting was done in different ways.

z-m-14-06.title: If there are twice as many people, will the job finish in half the time?
z-m-14-06.topic: Number of people working together and the time it takes (checking conditions)
z-m-14-06.goal: Find the conditions needed for the judgment "if the number of people doubles, the time halves" to hold, and revise your judgment when new information breaks a condition.
z-m-14-06.material: There is a job of pulling weeds in the school garden. They say that if 3 people pull for one hour every day, it takes 8 days. Jihun said, "If 6 people pull for one hour every day, there are twice as many people, so it will finish in 4 days!" The amount of weeds to pull is the same.
z-m-14-06.thinking.0: Finding what conditions must hold for the conclusion to follow
z-m-14-06.thinking.1: Judging whether new information changes the conditions
z-m-14-06.thinking.3: Writing a recommendation with conditions included
z-m-14-06.prereq.0: The idea that the amount of work grows as the number of people and the number of days worked grow (grade 5)
z-m-14-06.prereq.1: Simple word problems mixing multiplication and division (grade 5)
z-m-14-06.s.s1.prompt: What must be true for Jihun's "it will finish in 4 days" to be right? Choose everything that is needed.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.hint.0: Besides "the number of people doubled," write what must be the same in the two cases, one by one.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine a situation where the work does not shrink or the time changes even if the number of people grows.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.o.a: The 3 new people are in the same grade.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.r.a: This is information not directly related to the amount of work or the speed. Work out whether this information changes the time it takes.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.o.b: If more people work, the job finishes faster.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.r.b: The direction is right, but it is not the condition for "exactly half." Work out whether how much faster it gets is fixed.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.o.c: Everyone works at a similar speed.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.r.c: You thought that if each person's speed is different, the result can change.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.o.d: The weeds pulled by 6 people are twice as many as those pulled by 3 people.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.r.d: If the amount of work changes, it can take the same time even if more people join. Check whether it fits the first condition.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.o.e: Even with 6 people, they can divide the work and work for the same amount of time without getting in each other's way.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.r.e: You thought that even if there are more people, they must be able to divide the work and do it at the same time.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.o.f: The time worked per day is the same one hour with 3 people and with 6 people.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.r.f: You thought that the length of time worked must be the same to compare only the number of people.
z-m-14-06.s.s1.explain: Everyone must work at a similar speed, not get in each other's way and work at the same time by dividing the work, and work the same time each day for the time to be half when the number of people doubles. The problem already says the amount of weeds is the same.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.prompt: You find out that the garden has only 3 hoes and the weeds can be pulled only with hoes. If 6 people share the 3 hoes and work for one hour every day, about how many days will it take?
z-m-14-06.s.s2.hint.0: First write how many people can work at one time with 3 hoes.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.hint.1: If some people rest while the 6 people take turns, compare how the amount pulled per day differs from when there were 3 people.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.o.a: It is 4 days. The number of people doubles to 6, so it is cut in half regardless of the number of hoes.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.r.a: You did not check the rule "if the number of people grows, the time shrinks" against new information like the number of hoes.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.o.b: It takes longer than 4 days. Only 3 people work at the same time, so it will be around 8 days.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.r.b: You revised your judgment to reflect that the new information changes "the number of hands working at the same time."
z-m-14-06.s.s2.o.c: It is 6 days. Even with the hoes, it will take about the middle of 4 and 8 days.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.r.c: You set the new information to the middle value without a reason.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.o.d: We cannot know the exact number of days. We need to know more, such as whether pulling by hand is also possible.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.r.d: You pointed out that a condition not used in the problem can change the result. You saw that information is lacking, so it is a careful judgment.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.explain: If there are only 3 hoes, only 3 people work at the same time, so even with 6 people, it progresses only as much as 3 people working. So it takes longer than 4 days, and since some people rest, it is around 8 days. The judgment that "we need to know more, such as the way of pulling by hand" also has a basis.
z-m-14-06.s.s2.acc.0: The judgment that more conditions are needed, such as whether there are people who pull by hand, is also valid. It would be even better to confirm that when doing it with hoes only, it is around 8 days.
z-m-14-06.s.s3.prompt: Write what you would say to Jihun. Give one condition under which 6 people can finish in 4 days and one situation in which it might not finish in 4 days.
z-m-14-06.s.s3.hint.0: Try starting with "If ..., it is 4 days."
z-m-14-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think of a scene where having 6 people work becomes pointless, and write it in a sentence.
z-m-14-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If everyone works at the same speed, ...
z-m-14-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write separately the condition for it to be 4 days and the situation where it is not 4 days?
z-m-14-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain that the situation you wrote really makes the time longer?
z-m-14-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying without conditions things like "if there are twice as many people, the time is always half"?
z-m-14-06.s.s3.model.0: If everyone works at the same speed and can divide the work and do it at the same time, 6 people finish in 4 days. But if there are only 3 hoes, only 3 people work at the same time, so it takes longer than 4 days.
z-m-14-06.s.s3.model.1: For 6 people to finish in 4 days, each person's speed must be the same and they must not get in each other's way. If a new person is slow or they crowd into a narrow place and get in each other's way, it can take more than 4 days.
z-m-14-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: You gave a different situation as an example.

z-m-14-07.title: 40% and 25%: which class has more members?
z-m-14-07.topic: Ratio and actual amount: when the base quantities are different
z-m-14-07.goal: Show with examples you make yourself that the size of a ratio and the actual number of people can compare differently when the base quantity (total number of people) is different, and find why you must not estimate by the middle value when combining the ratios of two classes.
z-m-14-07.material: In the after-school reading club, 40% of the students in Class 3 and 25% of the students in Class 5 joined. You do not yet know the total number of students in the two classes. The number of students in a class is at least 15 and at most 50, and the number of students who joined is a natural number (a person cannot be cut in half).
z-m-14-07.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-14-07.thinking.1: Making examples that satisfy the conditions yourself
z-m-14-07.thinking.2: Finding the error in a generalization
z-m-14-07.prereq.0: The meaning of percentage and ratio (grade 6)
z-m-14-07.prereq.1: Finding the amount of a part from its ratio to the whole (grade 6)
z-m-14-07.s.s1.prompt: Which class has more students who joined?
z-m-14-07.s.s1.hint.0: Choose the total number of students in each of the two classes and find the number of students who joined.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.hint.1: Try choosing different numbers of students for Class 3 and Class 5 and see whether which one has more members changes.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.o.a: We cannot decide if we do not know the total number of students in the two classes.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.r.a: You judged that a ratio is a share of the whole, so to compare the number of students who joined, you need the total number of students.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.o.b: Class 3 has more. This is because 40% is greater than 25%.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.r.b: You compared only the size of the ratios. You did not check whether the total numbers of students in the two classes are the same.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.o.c: Class 5 has more. This is because the class with the lower ratio has more students.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.r.c: You guessed the opposite without checking evidence. Try a class with fewer students too.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.o.d: Class 3 will usually have more, but it is not certain. This is because 40% is much bigger.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.r.d: You thought the side with the bigger ratio is likely to have more. Test examples of a class with fewer students and a class with more students to check whether that is really so.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.o.e: They are the same. This is because in both classes only some of the students joined.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.r.e: Check whether the fact that it is "some" is a reason for the numbers of students who joined to be the same.
z-m-14-07.s.s1.explain: A ratio is a share of the whole, so to compare the number of students who joined, you need to know the total number of students in the two classes. For example, if Class 3 has 20 students, it is 8, and if Class 5 has 40 students, it is 10, so Class 5 can have more.
z-m-14-07.s.s2.prompt: Make three cases where more students from Class 5 joined than from Class 3. Class 3 has x students and Class 5 has y students. (The number of students who joined is a natural number.)
z-m-14-07.s.s2.hint.0: Try starting with a small number of students in Class 3 and a large number in Class 5.
z-m-14-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find the number of students who joined in each class and compare whether Class 5 is bigger than Class 3.
z-m-14-07.s.s2.ok.c1: Both classes have at least 15 and at most 50 students.
z-m-14-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of students in a class must be at least 15 and at most 50.
z-m-14-07.s.s2.ok.c2: 40% and 25% come out as whole numbers of students.
z-m-14-07.s.s2.fail.c2: For the number of students who joined to be a natural number, Class 3 must be a multiple of 5 and Class 5 must be a multiple of 4.
z-m-14-07.s.s2.fail.c3: With these numbers of students, Class 5 does not have more students who joined than Class 3. Find the number of students who joined in each of the two classes and compare.
z-m-14-07.s.s2.explain: For example, if Class 3 has 20 students, 8 joined, and if Class 5 has 36 students, 9 joined, so Class 5 has more. Class 3 with 15 (6 students) and Class 5 with 28 (7 students), and Class 3 with 25 (10 students) and Class 5 with 44 (11 students) also work. 20 and 32 give 8 for both, so it is not "more."
z-m-14-07.s.s3.prompt: Minho thought about the combined ratio of the two classes as below. Pick the wrong line.
z-m-14-07.s.s3.hint.0: Choose different numbers of students (for example, both classes have 20) and find the combined ratio with the same method.
z-m-14-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how the combined ratio changes when the numbers of students in the two classes at the start are different.
z-m-14-07.s.s3.line.0: Class 3 is 40% and Class 5 is 25%. The combined joining ratio of the two classes seems like it would be the middle value, 32.5%.
z-m-14-07.s.s3.line.1: Let's say Class 3 has 20 students and Class 5 has 40 students, and check.
z-m-14-07.s.s3.line.2: Class 3's members are 40% of 20, which is 8, and Class 5's members are 25% of 40, which is 10.
z-m-14-07.s.s3.line.3: Putting the two classes together, 18 out of 60 joined, so the joining ratio is 30%. It is not 32.5%.
z-m-14-07.s.s3.line.4: So the combined joining ratio of the two classes is always 30%, no matter how many students are in the classes.
z-m-14-07.s.s3.explain: Line 5 is wrong. Getting 30% in one case (20 and 40) does not mean every case is 30%. For example, if Class 3 has 20 and Class 5 has 20, then 8+5=13 out of 40 joined, so it is 32.5%.

z-m-14-08.title: What if we paint a big cube and split it into single blocks?
z-m-14-08.topic: A cube made of unit blocks and the number of painted faces
z-m-14-08.goal: As the number of blocks along one edge of a cube made of unit blocks changes, look at several cases to revise your predictions of how the number of blocks with each number of painted faces changes, and explain using structure (faces, edges, vertices).
z-m-14-08.material: Stack unit blocks (small cubes with an edge of 1 cm) to make a big cube with □ blocks along each edge. Paint all six outer faces of the big cube red (think of the face that touched the floor as painted too), then take all the blocks apart one by one. Then the blocks are sorted into those with 0, 1, 2, or 3 painted faces. Think only about cases where there are 3 or more blocks along one edge.
z-m-14-08.thinking.0: Predicting a rule from a few cases and testing it with a new case
z-m-14-08.thinking.1: Comparing the prediction that it grows steadily with a prediction based on structure
z-m-14-08.thinking.2: Telling apart cases where the number does not change from cases where it does
z-m-14-08.prereq.0: Faces, edges, and vertices of cuboids and cubes (grade 4-5)
z-m-14-08.prereq.1: Counting the number of blocks in a shape made of unit blocks (grade 5-6)
z-m-14-08.s.s1.prompt: As you see the information one piece at a time, predict the number of blocks with 1 painted face (and, at the end, the number of blocks with 3 painted faces). You do not have to change your first prediction. Decide for yourself whether the new information changes your judgment or whether it can stay the same.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write the newly given numbers in a table together with the number of blocks on an edge.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.hint.1: Picture one face of the big cube, take away one row along the edge, and count how many are left inside.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.info: You made it with 3 blocks along an edge (3×3×3, 27 in all), painted it, and took it apart, and there were 6 blocks with only 1 painted face. That is one in the middle of each of the six faces of the big cube.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: If you make it with 6 blocks along an edge (6×6×6, 216 in all), about how many blocks will have only 1 painted face?
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.after: It is hard to trust a rule from just one size. Let's count the cases with 4 and 5 blocks along an edge too.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 6. This is because the big cube has only 6 faces.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You looked only at the number of faces and did not think about the number of blocks on one face changing.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: About 12. The edge becomes 2 times as long, so the number also becomes about 2 times.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a proportional idea that if the length doubles, the number also doubles. You can test it with a new case.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: About 24. The area of one face becomes 4 times, so the number also becomes about 4 times.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought of the number of blocks on one face as an area.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is hard to estimate from just one size. We need to count other sizes too.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You think the evidence is still lacking and want to look at more cases.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.info: You made it with 4 blocks along an edge (4×4×4, 64 in all), and there were 24 blocks with only 1 painted face. On each face there are the 2×2=4 in the middle, for six faces. With 3 blocks along an edge it is 6, and with 4 it is 24.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: Seeing these two results, about how many blocks will have only 1 painted face when there are 6 blocks along an edge?
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.after: There are two ways to guess the rule. One is to see the amount of increase as steady, and one is to look directly at the shape of one face. Let's test with a third case.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: About 60. It went up by 18 from 3 to 4, so it goes up by 18 each time.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a prediction that sees the amount of increase in the two cases as staying the same. You can test it with the next case.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: About 96. Count the inside square of a face after taking away the border rows, and count six faces.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You predicted by directly counting using the structure of the cube (the inside square of one face).
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 12. It doubled from 3 to 6, so it is twice 6.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You are stating your first guess as it was, without reflecting the two results you just saw (6 → 24).
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.o.d: I don't know yet. I should also count the case of 5 blocks along an edge and check whether the rule is right.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a careful judgment that does not settle the rule from two cases and wants to test one more.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.info: You made it with 5 blocks along an edge (5×5×5, 125 in all), and there were 54 blocks with only 1 painted face. So far it is 6 (for 3 blocks), 24 (for 4 blocks), and 54 (for 5 blocks).
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now, about how many blocks will have only 1 painted face when there are 6 blocks along an edge?
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.after: Whether you look at the amount of increase (18, 30, 42) or the inside square of one face, 96 comes out. When two methods give the same value, the prediction becomes more trustworthy.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 60. I think it goes up by 18 each time, as before.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The amounts of increase, 18 and 30, were not steady. Check whether the earlier rule is also right for the new result.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 96. The amounts of increase, 18 and 30, grow by 12, so next you add 42.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You found the rule by also looking at how the amount of increase changes.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 78. Add 24, the middle of the increases 18 and 30, to 54.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The amount of increase is not steady, but you treated it as a middle value. Look at how the amount of increase changes.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 96. On each face, take away the border and count the inside 4×4=16, for six faces.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You counted directly using the structure of the cube and found the same value.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.o.e: You cannot be sure until you actually build 6×6×6 and count.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.r.e: This is a careful attitude that separates prediction from direct checking. It makes you think about how to check that the rule fits well.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.info: The number of blocks with 3 painted faces was 8 when there were 3, 4, and 5 blocks along an edge.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.ask: How many blocks have 3 painted faces when there are 6 blocks along an edge?
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.after: Blocks with 3 painted faces are only at the 8 vertices of the big cube. Even if the edge length changes, the number of vertices stays the same, 8.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.o.a: 16. It doubled from 3 to 6, so the number also doubles.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.r.a: You carried over, as it was, the experience of the number changing when the length changes with blocks painted on 1 face to the case of 3 painted faces.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.o.b: 8. This is because there is one at each of the 8 vertices of the big cube.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You explained why the number does not change using the structure of the cube (the number of vertices).
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.o.c: 24. It becomes 4 times, like the blocks painted on 1 face.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You applied the change from a different kind of block as it was.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.o.d: It was 8 all three times, so it seems like it will be 8, but we should also count the 6-block case.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.st.3.r.d: You looked at the results of all three cases and want to check carefully.
z-m-14-08.s.s1.reflect: The blocks with only one face painted went 6, 24, 54, 96 for 3, 4, 5, 6 blocks, growing much faster, not in proportion to the edge length. The blocks with three faces painted stayed at 8. Look back at what information changed your prediction (or whether it did not need to change), and when the method of predicting by the amount of increase and the method of predicting by structure gave the same value.
z-m-14-08.s.s2.prompt: In a big cube with 6 blocks along an edge, how many blocks have 2 painted faces? Explain how you know.
z-m-14-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write how many edges the big cube has and how many blocks lie along one edge.
z-m-14-08.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many of the blocks along one edge are at vertices and how many are the rest.
z-m-14-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does the method I wrote explain not only how to calculate but also where in the big cube those blocks are?
z-m-14-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that my method is right for other sizes (3 and 4 blocks)?
z-m-14-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check that the blocks with 0, 1, 2, and 3 painted faces add up to 216?
z-m-14-08.s.s2.model.0: It is 48. A cube has 12 edges, and of the 6 blocks along an edge, taking away the 2 at the ends (vertices) leaves 4 each, so 12×4=48.
z-m-14-08.s.s2.model.1: With 3 blocks along an edge it is 12, with 4 it is 24, and with 5 it is 36, so each time the edge gets one block longer, it goes up by 12. So with 6 it is 48. It also matches the total: 8+48+96+64=216.
z-m-14-08.s.s2.modelNote.1: You checked both the rule and the total number.

z-m-14-09.title: Estimating the area of a circle with a grid
z-m-14-09.topic: Estimating the area of a circle (counting grid squares)
z-m-14-09.goal: Using the squares that the circle completely contains on a grid and the squares it partly covers, say the range in which the area of the circle lies, and check your estimate by seeing how the range changes when the squares are made smaller.
z-m-14-09.material: A circle with a radius of 5 cm is drawn on grid paper where each square is 1 cm wide and 1 cm long (area 1 cm²). The center of the circle is at one vertex of the grid. There are 60 squares completely inside the circle, and including the squares that the circle's line passes through, there are 88 squares in all that are at least partly inside the circle. Assume you have not yet learned how to find the area of a circle.
z-m-14-09.thinking.0: Speaking in terms of a range instead of an exact value
z-m-14-09.thinking.1: Making several estimates that satisfy the conditions
z-m-14-09.thinking.2: Checking and revising an estimate with new information
z-m-14-09.prereq.0: The meaning of area and counting 1 cm² grid squares (grade 3-4)
z-m-14-09.prereq.1: Parts of a circle (radius, diameter) and the meaning of pi (grade 6, first semester)
z-m-14-09.s.s1.prompt: What can you say about the area of the circle from the result of this grid counting?
z-m-14-09.s.s1.hint.0: Draw it square by square and think about how the squares completely inside and the squares partly covered relate to the area of the circle.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.hint.1: Work out whether the area of the circle can be less than 60 and whether it can be more than 88.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.o.a: The area of the circle is 60 cm². Only the squares completely inside are in the circle.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.r.a: You missed that the squares the circle's line passes through also have a part that is inside the circle.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.o.b: The area of the circle is 88 cm². The squares the line passes through are all circle.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.r.b: You did not consider that the squares the line passes through are only partly inside the circle.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.o.c: The area of the circle is greater than 60 cm² and less than 88 cm².
z-m-14-09.s.s1.r.c: You used the area of the squares completely inside and the area of the squares at least partly inside to state a range.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.o.d: The area of the circle is exactly 74 cm². This is because it is the middle of 60 and 88.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.r.d: You asserted that the middle of the range is the exact value. There is no way to know whether the partly covered squares are half inside.
z-m-14-09.s.s1.explain: The circle is bigger than the 60 squares completely inside, and smaller than the 88 squares at least partly inside. So we can say it is greater than 60 cm² and less than 88 cm².
z-m-14-09.s.s2.prompt: Write three different values (in cm²) that you think are reasonable estimates of this circle's area. (Write them as whole numbers.)
z-m-14-09.s.s2.hint.0: Think of a few numbers greater than 60 and less than 88.
z-m-14-09.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how much, on average, of the 28 partly covered squares (88−60) might be inside, and decide on an estimate.
z-m-14-09.s.s2.ok.c1: It is greater than 60 and less than 88.
z-m-14-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The area of the circle must be greater than 60 cm² and less than 88 cm².

z-m-14-10.title: If you glue two boxes together, what happens to the surface area?
z-m-14-10.topic: Surface area of a solid made by joining shapes
z-m-14-10.goal: Find the error in the solution "just add the surface areas of each" when finding the surface area of a solid made by joining two cuboids, and judge the condition under which the position of the join affects the surface area.
z-m-14-10.material: Place a small cuboid B (4 cm wide, 6 cm long, 3 cm high) on the top face of a large cuboid A (10 cm wide, 6 cm long, 4 cm high) and glue them to make one solid. The whole bottom of B (4 cm wide, 6 cm long) touches the top face of A, and B's length of 6 cm is the same as A's length of 6 cm, so the front and back faces line up. You want to paint every face that shows on the outside of this solid (including the bottom face). "Surface area" is the sum of the areas of all the faces that show on the outside.
z-m-14-10.thinking.1: Judging whether the way (position) of joining changes the result
z-m-14-10.thinking.2: Reasoning how the conclusion changes when the conditions change
z-m-14-10.prereq.0: Finding the surface area of a cuboid (grade 5)
z-m-14-10.s.s1.prompt: Seohyeon found the surface area like this. Pick one wrong line.
z-m-14-10.s.s1.hint.0: Find which faces can no longer be seen from the outside when A and B are joined.
z-m-14-10.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the area of the faces that cannot be seen is included in each of 248 and 108.
z-m-14-10.s.s1.line.2: The surface area of the joined solid is the surface areas of A and B added together: 248+108=356 cm².
z-m-14-10.s.s1.line.3: So the area to paint is 356 cm².
z-m-14-10.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The part where A's top face and B's bottom face touch (4×6=24 cm²) cannot be seen from outside after joining. But 248 includes A's top face of 24 cm², and 108 includes B's bottom face of 24 cm², so the two hidden parts were not subtracted. 356−24−24=308 cm² is right, and the 356 cm² in the last line is wrong as a result.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.prompt: B can be attached anywhere as long as the whole bottom of B touches inside A's top face. Mingi glued B to the left end of A's top face, and Hayun glued it around the middle (in both, B's length is the same as A's length). How do the surface areas of the two solids compare?
z-m-14-10.s.s2.hint.0: Find the touching area for each of the two solids.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether, if the touching area is the same, the hidden area is also the same.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.o.a: Mingi's is smaller. This is because at the left end the faces line up, so more of it overlaps.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.r.a: You treated faces that look continuous on the same plane as the same as faces that are hidden. Even if they line up, the exposed area does not get smaller.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.o.b: Hayun's is bigger. This is because if you attach it to the middle, new edges appear on both sides of B.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.r.b: You treated more edges as the same as more surface area. Work it out with the areas of the faces.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.o.c: You cannot compare the two solids until you measure the position of the join exactly.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.r.c: Work out whether what you need to decide the surface area is the exact value of the position or the touching area.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.o.d: The surface areas of the two solids are the same. This is because the touching area is the same wherever it is attached.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.r.d: You compared by working out whether the area of the hidden faces is the same even when the position differs.
z-m-14-10.s.s2.explain: As long as the whole bottom of B touches inside A's top face, the touching area is 24 cm² wherever it is attached. So the hidden area is the same and the surface area is also the same, 308 cm².
z-m-14-10.s.s3.hint.0: Write the width and length of the part of B's bottom face that actually touches A's top face.
z-m-14-10.s.s3.hint.1: When the touching area is 24, compare how much was subtracted from 356.
z-m-14-10.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., It is not the same. Because ...

z-m-14-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write with numbers that the touching area changed from 24 cm² to 6 cm²?
z-m-14-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write exactly what is subtracted from 356 and by how much?
z-m-14-10.s.s3.model.0: It is not the same. If 3 cm sticks out, the touching face with A is only 1×6=6 cm², so you subtract 12, twice 6, from the sum of the two surface areas, 356, to get 344 cm².
z-m-14-10.s.s3.model.1: It changes. The touching area goes down from 24 to 6, so the hidden area goes down from 48 to 12, and the surface area gets bigger: 356−12=344.
z-m-14-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: You explained with the change in the hidden area.
z-m-14-10.s.s3.prompt: Hayun slid B sideways and glued it so that 3 cm of B's 4 cm width sticks out past the top face of A and only 1 cm sits on top of A's top face (B's depth is the same as A's depth). Is the surface area then the same as when B is glued inside A's top face? Find the value and write the reason.

z-m-14-11.title: Looking from above it is a circle. What shape could it be?
z-m-14-11.topic: Cylinders, cones, and spheres: their shapes depending on the direction you look
z-m-14-11.goal: Understand that the shape seen from one direction may not decide the solid, choose the information needed to decide the shape as one, and make a question that tells them apart.
z-m-14-11.material: A solid shape is on a desk. This shape is one of a cylinder, a cone, or a sphere. The cylinder and cone are set upright with their round base on the floor (the cone's pointed tip is up), and the sphere is simply resting there. A friend looked straight down from above and said, "I see a circle!"
z-m-14-11.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-14-11.thinking.1: Finding a counterexample (a different shape that looks the same)
z-m-14-11.thinking.2: Designing a question that tells them apart
z-m-14-11.prereq.0: Learning the shapes of cylinders, cones, and spheres (grade 6)
z-m-14-11.prereq.1: Imagining solids seen from above, the front, and the side
z-m-14-11.s.s1.prompt: Can you tell which shape it is from the statement alone that the shape seen from above is a circle?
z-m-14-11.s.s1.hint.0: Picture and draw the shape of each of the three solids seen from above.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.hint.1: Group together the shapes that look the same from above.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.o.a: It is a cylinder. If the shape seen from above is a circle, it is a cylinder.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.r.a: You did not check how a cone or a sphere looks from above.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.o.b: It looks like a circle whether it is a cylinder, a cone, or a sphere.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.r.b: You pictured and compared the shape of each of the three seen from above.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.o.c: It is a sphere. The only shape that looks like a circle is a sphere.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.r.c: From the fact that a sphere looks like a circle from every direction, you said backward that if it looks like a circle, it is a sphere.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.o.d: It is a cone. If the pointed tip is up, the shape seen from above is a circle.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.r.d: You did not check the shapes of the cylinder and sphere seen from above.
z-m-14-11.s.s1.explain: An upright cylinder seen from above shows the circle of its top face, a cone with its point up shows the circle of its base, and a sphere shows a circle. So you cannot tell the three shapes apart from the shape seen from above alone.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.prompt: In addition to the fact that the shape seen from above is a circle, knowing which one of the following pieces of information would decide the shape as one? Choose all that fit.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.hint.0: Picture how the shape seen from the front differs for each of the three shapes.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.hint.1: Count, one by one, how many shapes satisfy each piece of information.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.o.a: The shape seen from the front is a rectangle.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.r.a: You chose it by working out that only one shape has a rectangle as its front view.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.o.b: The diameter of the circle seen from above is 6 cm.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.r.b: You can make a cylinder, a cone, and a sphere all the same size. Size cannot tell the kinds of shapes apart.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.o.c: The shape seen from the front is a triangle.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.r.c: You chose it by working out that only one shape has a triangle as its front view.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.o.d: The height of the shape is 6 cm.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.r.d: You can make a cylinder and a cone with the same height, and a sphere with a diameter of 6 cm also has a height of 6 cm. Height cannot decide the shape.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.o.e: The shape seen from the front is a circle.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.r.e: You chose it by working out that only one shape has a circle as its front view.
z-m-14-11.s.s2.explain: If the front view is a rectangle it is a cylinder, if it is a triangle it is a cone, and if it is a circle it is a sphere. Size (diameter) or height can be made the same for all three shapes, so they cannot decide the shape.
z-m-14-11.s.s3.prompt: You want to give a friend a quiz. Make one question that tells apart these three shapes that are circles from above, and write how the answer comes out for each shape.
z-m-14-11.s.s3.hint.0: First draw the shape of a cylinder seen from the front.
z-m-14-11.s.s3.hint.1: Find a direction in which the answers for the three shapes become different.
z-m-14-11.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., I'll ask for the shape seen from the front ...
z-m-14-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the answer to my question come out different for all three shapes?
z-m-14-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do the question about the front view and the question about the side view give the same result?
z-m-14-11.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think again about whether the shape seen from above can be used as a question?
z-m-14-11.s.s3.model.0: I'll ask what the shape seen from the front is. A cylinder would answer a rectangle, a cone a triangle, and a sphere a circle.
z-m-14-11.s.s3.model.1: I'll ask about the shape seen from the side. A sphere is a circle, a cylinder is a rectangle (or square), and a cone is a triangle, so they can be told apart in one go.
z-m-14-11.s.s3.modelNote.1: You said that the result is the same even if the direction is the side.

z-m-14-12.title: The length of string tying three cans
z-m-14-12.topic: Length of a perimeter using circumference (tying cans)
z-m-14-12.goal: Estimate the length of the string that goes around touching cans by splitting it into straight parts and round parts, and compare how the length of the string changes depending on the arrangement.
z-m-14-12.material: Stand 3 cylinder-shaped cans with a diameter of 6 cm and tie them with one string pulled tight once around the middle of the cans' height. The string touches the cans' sides with no gaps, and do not think about string used for the knot. Calculate pi as 3.14. There are two ways to place the cans. (가) Stand the three cans side by side in a row, touching. (나) Stand the three cans in a triangle shape so that they all touch each other.
z-m-14-12.thinking.0: Thinking of the perimeter of a shape by splitting it into parts
z-m-14-12.thinking.1: Finding and fixing an error in a solution
z-m-14-12.thinking.2: Comparing two arrangements and judging with evidence
z-m-14-12.prereq.1: The relationship between the diameter and radius of a circle
z-m-14-12.s.s1.prompt: Before calculating the length of string needed when tying with (가) and with (나), estimate first. Which one seems longer?
z-m-14-12.s.s1.hint.0: Draw the three circles seen from above and draw a line along the path the string takes.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.hint.1: Mark the points where the string changes from a round part to a straight part and count how many straight parts there are.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.o.a: (나) is longer. It bends in three directions, so the string passes through more round parts.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.r.a: You thought more bends make it longer. Work it out by adding up the lengths where the string passes along round parts.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.o.b: The two ways are the same. Either way, it wraps all around the 3 cans.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.r.b: You missed that the string does not wrap all the way around the cans; between cans that touch, it goes straight without following the outline.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.o.c: (가) is longer. The part that goes straight between the cans is longer in (가).
z-m-14-12.s.s1.r.c: You split the string into round parts and straight parts and compared the straight parts of the two arrangements.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.o.d: We cannot compare until we know the height of the cans.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.r.d: The length of one trip around the string is decided by the arrangement seen from above. Think about whether the height changes the length of the string.
z-m-14-12.s.s1.explain: The string can be split into the round parts of the cans and the straight parts between the cans. In both arrangements, the round parts together make the circumference of one can, and the straight part is longer in (가). So (가) seems longer. You can check this estimate by calculating.
z-m-14-12.s.s2.prompt: Hansol found the length of string for tying with (가) as below. Pick one wrong line.
z-m-14-12.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine the line joining the centers of the cans at the two ends and count how many diameters long it is.
z-m-14-12.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the middle can changes the length of the straight parts.
z-m-14-12.s.s2.line.0: The places the string touches can be divided into the round parts of the cans at the two ends and the straight parts at the top and bottom.
z-m-14-12.s.s2.line.1: Putting together the round parts of the cans at the two ends gives the circumference of one can, 6×3.14=18.84 cm.
z-m-14-12.s.s2.line.2: The straight part on top has 3 cans side by side, so its length is 6 cm. The bottom is 6 cm too.
z-m-14-12.s.s2.line.3: The total length of the string is 18.84+6+6=30.84 cm.
z-m-14-12.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The straight part on top equals the distance between the centers of the cans at the two ends, so with 3 cans in a row it is 2 diameters, 12 cm. The bottom is also 12 cm, so 18.84+12+12=42.84 cm is right, and the 30.84 cm in line 4 is wrong as a result.
z-m-14-12.s.s3.prompt: Find the length of string when tying with (나), compare it with the length when tying with (가) (42.84 cm), and write which is shorter and by how much, with the reason.
z-m-14-12.s.s3.hint.0: Write what shape you get when you join the centers of the three cans in (나) and how long one side is.
z-m-14-12.s.s3.hint.1: Write the sum of the straight parts and the sum of the round parts separately and compare.
z-m-14-12.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If you tie them in a triangle, ...
z-m-14-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In (나), did you write how many straight parts there are and how many cm each is?
z-m-14-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing why the round parts are the same length in the two arrangements?
z-m-14-12.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you compare whether your first estimate (step 1) and the calculated result are the same?
z-m-14-12.s.s3.model.0: If you tie them in a triangle, the straight parts are 3 parts of 6 cm each, 18 cm, and the round part is 18.84 cm, so it is 36.84 cm. A row is 42.84 cm, so the triangle uses 6 cm less.
z-m-14-12.s.s3.model.1: The straight parts in a row are 2 parts of 12 cm each, 24 cm, but in a triangle they are 3 parts of 6 cm each, 18 cm, so the triangle is 6 cm shorter. The round parts together in both make the circumference of one can, 18.84 cm, so they are the same.
z-m-14-12.s.s3.modelNote.1: You explained that the round parts are the same and only the straight parts differ, so there is a difference.

z-m-14-13.title: Comparing the areas of shapes made from the same wire
z-m-14-13.topic: Area of shapes with the same perimeter (rectangles and a circle)
z-m-14-13.goal: Confirm with examples you make yourself that rectangles with the same perimeter can have very different areas, and tell apart what you can say within the range you tested from what you still cannot settle.
z-m-14-13.material: Eunu has a piece of wire that is 62.8 cm long. He wants to use all of this wire, with no overlap and nothing left over, to make a shape (do not think about the thickness of the wire). Eunu said, "The wire is the same length, so whatever shape I make, the area will be about the same." Calculate pi as 3.14.
z-m-14-13.thinking.0: Testing a claim with many cases
z-m-14-13.thinking.1: Making examples that satisfy the conditions yourself
z-m-14-13.thinking.2: Telling apart how far the evidence goes
z-m-14-13.prereq.0: Perimeter and area of a rectangle (grade 4)
z-m-14-13.prereq.1: Pi and finding the circumference and area of a circle (grade 6)
z-m-14-13.s.s1.prompt: Make three different sizes of rectangles from the wire that have an area of at least 230 cm². (width w, length h, unit cm, up to one decimal place)
z-m-14-13.s.s1.hint.0: First write what the width and length must add up to for the perimeter to be 62.8 cm.
z-m-14-13.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate a few areas when the width and length are similar and when they are very different, and compare.
z-m-14-13.s.s1.fail.c1: The width and length must be greater than 0.
z-m-14-13.s.s1.ok.c2: It is up to one decimal place.
z-m-14-13.s.s1.fail.c2: Please write only up to one decimal place.
z-m-14-13.s.s1.ok.c3: The whole wire is used and the perimeter is 62.8 cm.
z-m-14-13.s.s1.ok.c4: The area is at least 230 cm².
z-m-14-13.s.s1.fail.c4: The area is less than 230 cm². Try making the difference between the width and length smaller.
z-m-14-13.s.s1.explain: The sum of the width and length is 62.8÷2=31.4 cm. With width 15.7 and length 15.7, the area is 246.49 cm². 15×16.4=246 cm², 14×17.4=243.6 cm², 13×18.4=239.2 cm², and 12×19.4=232.8 cm² are also at least 230 cm². With width 10 and length 21.4, it is 214 cm², which falls short of 230 cm².
z-m-14-13.s.s2.prompt: You compared the rectangles calculated above with a circle made from the same wire (radius 10 cm, perimeter 62.8 cm, area 314 cm²). Choose everything you can say from the calculations so far.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.hint.0: Mark one by one whether each sentence is confirmed by "the numbers I calculated."
z-m-14-13.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether there are shapes left that were not compared, and look again at the sentences that include "all" or "always."
z-m-14-13.s.s2.o.a: If the perimeter is the same 62.8 cm, the area is the same for any shape.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.r.a: You treated having the same perimeter as having the same area. Check whether the areas you calculated are the same as each other.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.o.b: Even rectangles with a perimeter of 62.8 cm can have very different areas.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.r.b: This is a conclusion from comparing the areas of several rectangles.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.o.c: Among all shapes with a perimeter of 62.8 cm, the square has the greatest area.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.r.c: You widened the biggest of the rectangles you tested to all shapes. Compare with the area of the circle.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.o.d: Among rectangles, the smaller the difference between the width and length, the greater the area tends to be.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.r.d: You tried to find a rule by organizing the areas of several cases.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.o.e: It has already been proved that the circle is the widest of all shapes.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.r.e: You widened the result of comparing a few shapes to all shapes. There are shapes left that were not compared.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.o.f: This circle (area 314 cm²) is wider than all the rectangles made above.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.r.f: You compared the area of the circle and the areas of the rectangles with numbers.
z-m-14-13.s.s2.explain: Even with the same perimeter, the area of a rectangle changes a lot (for example, 246.49 and 42), and the smaller the difference between width and length, the greater the area. The circle, at 314 cm², is wider than the rectangles made. But since only a few shapes were compared, "the circle is the widest of all shapes" is not settled, and "the square is the widest" is wrong too.
z-m-14-13.s.s3.prompt: What would you say to Eunu? Show with numbers that Eunu's statement is not right, and write separately what you can say for sure from the calculations so far and what you still do not know.
z-m-14-13.s.s3.hint.0: Write down the area of the square made above and the area of a very long, thin rectangle, one each.
z-m-14-13.s.s3.hint.1: Write in one sentence each what you can say "for sure" and what you "still" do not know.
z-m-14-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are the two areas you gave really very different when compared?
z-m-14-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write separately "what I can say for sure" and "what I still do not know"?
z-m-14-13.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid asserting that the circle is the widest?
z-m-14-13.s.s3.model.0: No. Even if the perimeter is 62.8 cm, width 15.7 and length 15.7 give an area of 246.49, but width 30 and length 1.4 give an area of 42, so they are very different. z-m-14-14.title: Rewriting the ribbon instructions for tying a gift box
z-m-14-14.topic: Lengths of a cuboid and the length of ribbon (rewriting instructions)
z-m-14-14.goal: Learn how to find the length by following the path the ribbon really takes, and rewrite the wrong instructions into correct ones.
z-m-14-14.material: The gift box is a cuboid that is 20 cm wide, 15 cm long, and 10 cm high. You want to tie this box with ribbon in a cross shape. The ribbon crosses at the center of the top face of the box at right angles, goes straight down along the side faces, and crosses again at the center of the bottom face. One strand goes around the box once in the width direction and the other goes around once in the length direction. Do not think about the ribbon's thickness, and use an extra 25 cm for the knot and for making the bow.
z-m-14-14.thinking.1: Making sizes that satisfy the conditions yourself
z-m-14-14.thinking.2: Rewriting an explanation to suit the reader
z-m-14-14.prereq.0: Width, length, height, and position of faces of a cuboid (grade 4-5)
z-m-14-14.s.s1.prompt: Soyoung found the length of ribbon like this. Pick one wrong line.
z-m-14-14.s.s1.hint.0: Trace with your finger which faces of the box one strand of ribbon passes over in order.
z-m-14-14.s.s1.hint.1: In that length, count how many times each of the width, length, and height is included.
z-m-14-14.s.s1.line.0: Think that the ribbon winds along the edges of the box. A cuboid has 12 edges.
z-m-14-14.s.s1.line.1: There are 4 width edges, 4 length edges, and 4 height edges, so 4×(20+15+10)=180 cm.
z-m-14-14.s.s1.line.2: Adding the 25 cm for the knot and bow gives 180+25=205 cm needed.
z-m-14-14.s.s1.explain: It is wrong from line 1. A ribbon tied in a cross does not follow the edges; it passes through the centers of the top face and bottom face. So the 180 cm in line 2 and the 205 cm in line 3 are wrong too. One trip in the width direction is 20+10+20+10=60 cm, one trip in the length direction is 15+10+15+10=50 cm, so 60+50+25=135 cm is right.
z-m-14-14.s.s2.prompt: The ribbon shop has only one piece of ribbon, 120 cm long, left. Make three different sizes of cuboid box that can be tied with this one piece of ribbon in the same way as above (cross shape, 25 cm knot) and have a volume of at least 1500 cm³. (width a ≥ length b ≥ height h, all natural numbers of at least 5, unit cm)
z-m-14-14.s.s2.hint.0: Using the method you found above, set the width, length, and height and first calculate how much ribbon is needed.
z-m-14-14.s.s2.hint.1: Keep the ribbon from going over 120 cm while changing the width, length, and height, and compare the volumes.
z-m-14-14.s.s2.fail.c1: It must be width ≥ length ≥ height and the height must be at least 5.
z-m-14-14.s.s2.ok.c3: It can be tied with 120 cm of ribbon.
z-m-14-14.s.s2.fail.c3: The ribbon (one trip in the width direction + one trip in the length direction + 25 cm knot) goes over 120 cm.
z-m-14-14.s.s2.ok.c4: The volume is at least 1500 cm³.
z-m-14-14.s.s2.fail.c4: The volume is less than 1500 cm³. Try making the box bigger or changing its shape.
z-m-14-14.s.s2.explain: The length of ribbon is (width×2+height×2)+(length×2+height×2)+25 = width×2+length×2+height×4+25. To be 120 cm or less, width×2+length×2+height×4 must be 95 or less. For example, 15×15×8 needs 117 cm of ribbon and has a volume of 1800 cm³. 20×12×6 needs 113 cm of ribbon but its volume is 1440 cm³, so it does not work.
z-m-14-14.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Soyoung's explanation as gift-wrapping instructions that classmates will read. So that it can be used even if the size of the box changes, tell where the ribbon goes, how many times each of the width, length, and height is counted, and how to handle the length used for the knot.

z-m-14-14.s.s3.model.0: The ribbon does not follow the edges; it passes through the center of the top face and the center of the bottom face. One time it passes the width of the top face, the height of a side face, the width of the bottom face, and the height of the opposite side face, so it is (width×2+height×2). The other time it is (length×2+height×2). Add the two times and add the length for the knot. For this box it is 60+50+25=135 cm.
z-m-14-14.s.s3.model.1: The ribbon goes in a cross through the centers of the top and bottom faces of the box, not along the edges. One trip in the width direction counts the width 2 times and the height 2 times, and one trip in the length direction counts the length 2 times and the height 2 times, so together it is width×2+length×2+height×4. Then add the length for the knot.
